html:
Reviewer’s comments

Reviewer: myself, 1,779 days later.

Date of review: Sunday, December 30, 2018. Overcast.


Foreword: I started a PhD in Germany in 2013 and graduated in 2018. All through the PhD, I kept a diary written only for myself. Now, through those diaries, I’m looking back on the 1,800-plus days of my PhD, my days before thirty, and holding a time-traveling conversation with myself. Let five years of growing up serve as a warning to the world: be kind to every lovable, long-suffering PhD student.

I really love the big floor-to-ceiling window in my new office. Look up and you can see blue sky and white clouds outside (on a day like today, of course), and you can see far into the distance, as if I could go there, as if I were still back in China, still on my university campus.

Reviewer’s comments: The opening lacks originality. The style follows the lyrical prose essay that sells so well on the gaokao, China’s college entrance exam.


These past few days I’ve been getting better bit by bit, gradually climbing out of the slump of last week and the end of the week before, slowly finding my rhythm again and calming down enough to get things done. That stretch was probably the lowest point of my four months abroad. Suddenly I had no confidence in anything. In research I’m a total rookie: there is so, so much I don’t know and so, so much to learn. My schedule is packed, and yet actually doing any of it is so hard I don’t know where to begin. When I work I can’t concentrate at all, and my efficiency is frighteningly low. Then I get really anxious, and so begins the viscous circle.

Reviewer’s comments:
Typo: that’s “vicious circle,” not “viscous.” Mind your spelling.
What the author didn’t know at the time was that this slump was only one of many in his PhD, and not even the lowest one. Does hearing that make the author of back then feel any better?
His master’s project wasn’t in his own field, and his advisor wasn’t much help, so the master’s project was entirely DIY, and of course he taught himself everything. His PhD application was naturally related to his master’s project, but mostly he was interested in the field, and so he got into an institute working in it. But the project he ended up with wasn’t the one he had originally proposed, nor in the direction of his master’s, so once again he started from scratch. (And this was only the beginning: his Marie Curie project as a researcher afterward, and then his job, were in different directions again…)
The German PhD colleagues he faced had all been at the institute for 5+ years: bachelor’s thesis, then a bachelor’s Hiwi job (student assistant), then the master’s thesis, then a master’s Hiwi job, and finally the PhD. So even though they too were just starting their PhDs, they outclassed him in every way, whether in understanding the topic, knowing their way around the lab or knowing their colleagues. Not to mention the language: it was their mother tongue… Instead of honoring the fine tradition of keeping your head down and quietly making your fortune, he failed to see the situation for what it was, looked down on himself, and needlessly crushed his own motivation.


As for German, maybe the novelty has worn off, or maybe I’ve learned too few new things lately to keep up with a psychological need that grows over time. On top of that, my officemate Amu has a remarkable gift for languages. So every time he is laughing and chatting away with the Germans while I stand by at a loss, a powerful sense of inferiority and helplessness wells up in me.

Reviewer’s comments: Insufficient background given for the gossip.
Amu was the author’s officemate, a guy from the Middle East who arrived in Germany a month before the author and had already passed A1 German by the time the author showed up. A language fanatic, and the human specimen with the least social awkwardness the author has ever come across. His trick for breaking awkward silences and learning German fast: play the fool, keep insisting he was stupid, ask all kinds of questions, and change the subject constantly. Even the author, a Northeasterner, from a part of China famous for its funny people, had fewer humor bacteria growing on him than Amu, and faced with Germans, cool on the outside and wild on the inside, he was just as dumbfounded.
Under his influence, and having always been interested in languages, the author also threw himself into a rather crazy German-learning campaign. (He didn’t know then that Amu would become his best friend during his years abroad. Amu is one of the main characters of my PhD diaries; more about him in later entries.) In hindsight it cost a lot of precious research time and pushed back my graduation, but I don’t regret it. The best way to understand a country and its culture is to learn its language. All the more so in Germany: you can survive without German, no problem, but “danger” will come at you from every direction, and the Germans will look down on you deep inside. So I made a vow: learn your German and the world is your oyster! Defend my thesis in German! (Didn’t happen.)
More of my German-learning stories and gripes: https://www.zhihu.com/question/22249732/answer/559778873


This has a lot to do with the fierce pride that comes from my competitive streak since childhood: whatever it is, I have to measure myself against other people. Or rather, my experience is still shallow, and I have never had to survive among people who are truly talented. Even in my master’s I wasn’t in the strongest program, so the sense of superiority I’d had since I was a kid never diminished one bit. Taking the TOEFL, winning a scholarship, going abroad: everything I did seemed to earn praise and compliments. It never once occurred to me how dangerous that is! It made me a bit too big for my boots and kept me in a permanent state of self-satisfaction and self-intoxication. At the same time, my undergraduate program wasn’t a strong one, which left a deep-seated sense of inferiority, and so I ended up with a contradictory personality. If someone makes a joke at my expense about my research, for example, I can laugh it off on the surface, but inside I replay it over and over. It seems I have never really thought about this seriously. What dreadful, ridiculous vanity and hypocrisy!

Reviewer’s comments: Thus began a five-year journey of soul-searching self-discovery. Smash the Four Olds, as the Cultural Revolution slogan had it, and reboot…


So my so-called “slump” was inevitable: even if it hadn’t happened recently, it would have come sooner or later. Because can’t say things clearly in German, gets nervous speaking it, which leads to no confidence, which leads to dreading it the next time, which turns into a vicious circle, and what was bad to begin with gets even worse.

Reviewer’s comments: Unclear subject; sentences too long. Recommend breaking long sentences into short ones.
PS: If you can’t even write clear Chinese, how do you expect to speak good German?!
To this day, the author still can’t speak German with complete ease. He is always thinking about the grammar and trying to be accurate, which takes up too much of his brain’s CPU. Since he left Germany, his German has been going steadily downhill. And his Dutch hasn’t improved one bit; he has never felt much of an urge to learn it. I have to admit, I’ve been spoiled by the Dutch and their superb English and international outlook…


Later, when I talked it over with my wife, she said I was being too impatient, and that I shouldn’t keep comparing myself with others all the time.


In fact, beyond that personality of mine, or rather within it, lies an extreme concern with other people’s attitudes and opinions. So I second-guess, then get depressed, and that drags down both my productivity and my quality of life.

Reviewer’s comments: Strongly agree. Take yourself too seriously and life gets exhausting. A PhD is a marathon. There are chances to collaborate and to exchange ideas at meetings, but most of the time it’s a one-man battle, and only you really know what you are doing. Years of this cloistered slog breed a little arrogance and pride that keep colliding and clashing.

So my problems are obvious:

  1. Not good enough, and not wanting anyone to find out;
  2. Caring too much about what others think;
  3. Too impatient, unable to settle down.
Reviewer’s comments: Well said!


Really, doing one thing each day, steadily, and learning a little something, is progress. The road through a PhD is long; without a steady, calm heart it’s bound to be hard. Look at it another way: just do your best. What potential a person has, how much they get done and how much they achieve really does vary from person to person, and it’s hard to say. Or perhaps it’s easy to know, because it was all arranged long ago?


So: do a little every day, be happy about my progress and so want to keep progressing, without arrogance, without impatience, without forcing things, and look at everything with a calm heart. Don’t fuss over every little thing; open my heart to every matter and every person.

Reviewer’s comments: Not a vector graphic. Please resubmit.


“When time slowly fades away, and the world becomes the past…”

Reviewer’s comments: In search of spiritual comfort, the author read widely at the time. The lyric comes from a lovely Christian song, “A Hill Called Golgotha.”


When time and space have both receded, what does anything in front of me amount to?

Reviewer’s comments: Having ascended to the eleventh dimension to talk himself into being good. Well done!
Reviewer’s concluding remarks:
As the opening entry of the PhD diaries, this one already shows the author displaying the periodic anxiety typical of PhD students: plenty of inner drama, fierce internal conflict, searching self-criticism. This cycle (symptoms – self-criticism – back to full health – symptoms – self-criticism – back to full health – …) is spread unevenly across a PhD, and in the course of endlessly asking himself why, knowing all the right answers, he still can’t live his life right, a PhD student grows wild. One moment you feel like a dazzling genius, the next like a total loser. Fortunately, he regularly analyzed his own state of mind and was not ruled by his emotions. Whenever negative feelings came up, he either wrote in his diary, or found someone to talk to, or played a game of basketball: just find a way out. That is how he kept his passion for learning and eventually graduated in good health. I say in good health rather than successfully because, academically, the author didn’t publish many papers, so it doesn’t count as a success. Non-academically, the author mastered a second foreign language, made a whole crowd of friends, traveled to cities big and small all over Europe, actively built a network in academia and stayed mentally healthy: things the author considers more important than papers.
A PhD is tough, but it’s very worthwhile, especially abroad. Leaving aside the degree premium (something employers value more and more), the PhD experience is one of a kind. Learning how to learn is a precious skill for PhD students in every field; more importantly, the training in willpower before thirty pays off for the rest of your life.
